fix(desktop): eliminate concurrent-write race, harden error handling

Critical: writeFileDurable/writeFileDurableSync shared a fixed
`${finalPath}.tmp` temp path, so overlapping writers opened the same
inode. The loser's bytes could land in the file the winner had already
renamed into place, even after the loser's own promise rejected — a
reproduced case where the on-disk content matched a write whose
promise had thrown ENOENT. Give every call a unique temp path
(pid + uuid); worst case now degrades to an ordinary last-rename-wins
lost update, never torn content.

Also: swallow close() failures in the finally blocks so they don't
mask the real write/sync error (JS `finally` always overrides `try`'s
error), and retry renames that fail with EBUSY/EPERM on Windows only,
where transient file locks from AV/backup/indexer handles are common.

Test temp-file assertions now scan the directory for any `*.tmp` file
instead of checking the old fixed name, since that literal path can no
longer exist. Added a case pinning down that overlapping writes never
produce torn content.

that assignment through LaunchServices; when the running executable lives
inside an .app bundle, the call registers the process as a foreground
application. The packaged child runs Electron's own binary, which is inside
JadeAI.app, so it earned a dock tile of its own. ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE does not
help — it suppresses Chromium startup, not libuv's title call.

no LaunchServices entry; adding a single `process.title = ...` produces one
with `bundle path=/Applications/JadeAI.app`. Fixed by preloading
resources/next-title-guard.js via `node -r`, which shadows the property with a
plain accessor. Reads still return the last assigned value, so nothing
observable from JS changes — only the LaunchServices side effect is dropped.

Closing the window left the app resident. The macOS stay-alive convention suits
apps that are cheap to keep around; this one holds a Next server and an open
SQLite handle for a window that is no longer there. window-all-closed now
quits on every platform, and the `activate` re-open handler is gone with it.

Also fixes .gitignore, where fab1662 appended `release/` to a file with no
trailing newline and produced the dead entry `testrelease/` — leaving both
`release/` and `test` unignored.

next-server; /api/health, /zh/dashboard, /api/resume and /api/auth/session all

holding the port, and window state was flushed on the way out.

fix(desktop): stabilise the loopback port and close three teardown gaps

The reported symptom was the onboarding tour reappearing on every launch. The
cause is not in the tour code, which is correct: allocateLoopbackPort() picks a
new port every launch, the port is part of the page's origin, and Chromium
partitions localStorage by origin — so the renderer got a brand-new empty
storage area each time. The tour flag was collateral damage; the same mechanism
was also silently discarding the saved AI API keys and the dashboard view
preference. resolveServerPort now persists the port and reuses it while it is
still bindable, falling back to a fresh one when taken (failing to start is
worse than losing web storage for one session).

Also closes the three lifecycle gaps recorded earlier:

- Signals never reached will-quit, so kill, system shutdown, Ctrl+C in the dev
  terminal and the dev loop's own restart all skipped the settings flush and
  left the Next server behind. SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP now route through
  app.quit(), with a 3s watchdog — installing a handler suppresses the default
  "just die", so a wedged quit would otherwise hang forever.

- The Next child is spawned into its own process group and torn down as a tree
  (taskkill /T on Windows), so teardown no longer depends on Next forwarding
  the signal itself.

- sweepStaleDurableWriteTemps reclaims temps orphaned by a death between write
  and rename, which nothing cleaned up. Bounded streaming scan rather than
  readdirSync, which would materialise the whole listing — worst in exactly the
  case being cleaned up. The age cutoff is the safety argument: a fresh temp may
  belong to a live writer. Deliberately omits orca's "skip own pid" companion,
  since pid reuse would turn a reclaimable orphan into a permanent leak.

One correction to an earlier report: "killing next dev orphans the next-server
grandchild" does not reproduce. SIGTERM to next dev is forwarded and both exit
cleanly, port released; only SIGKILL orphans the grandchild. The residue
observed earlier was the will-quit gap above, where nothing signalled the child
at all. The group kill is redundancy, not the fix for that.

The `-r <path>` preload added in the previous commit is replaced with
`--require=<path>` as a single argv element: next dev re-execs node and
forwards these flags through NODE_OPTIONS, which rejects the short form
outright, killing the dev server. Production never re-execs, so this only
showed up in dev.

Verified on the repackaged app across three launches: same origin port each
time, tour flag and marker written on launch 1 still readable on launch 3, a
planted stale temp swept while the .bak sidecar survived, SIGTERM flushing

ci(desktop): build and release the client from ds-* tags

Desktop releases get their own pipeline, separate from the web image.

  push to desktop   -> build on all three targets, no release
  push a ds-* tag   -> build, then publish a GitHub Release with the installers

The web image workflow already could not fire on ds-* tags — its filter is
`v*` and `ds-v0.0.1` starts with a d — but that was incidental rather than
stated, so the job now also carries an explicit guard. Widening the tag filter
later cannot silently push a web image (and overwrite `latest`) for a client
release.

macOS arm64 and x64 build on separate runners because native modules cannot be
cross-packaged. This is not theoretical: Next's file tracer prunes
better-sqlite3's prebuilds down to the build host's triple, so an x64 dmg built
on an arm64 machine ships an arm64 binary, packages cleanly, and fails on first
launch. afterPack now verifies the prebuild matches the TARGET platform and
arch — confirmed by running `--mac --x64` on this arm64 machine, which now
fails the build with "Missing better-sqlite3 prebuild for darwin-x64" instead
of producing a broken dmg.

The prebuild lookup no longer hardcodes a version or a pnpm path: CI installs
with node-linker=hoisted so the tree copied into the app has no links to
survive (Windows junctions are absolute and would bake in the build machine's
paths), while a local `pnpm dist:mac` keeps pnpm's isolated layout. Both
layouts have to pass.

electron-builder runs with --publish never so it cannot upload on its own when
building from a tag; the release job is the single place that publishes, and it
refuses to publish unless all three installers are present — a release carrying
only the macOS build is harder to notice than an outright failure.

Windows ships an NSIS per-user installer with a directory choice rather than a
one-click: the binary is unsigned, so a visible install flow that needs no UAC
prompt is the one people will actually accept.

Verified locally: the arm64 dmg still builds and afterPack reports the target
triple; both workflow files parse and their triggers, matrix and gating
resolve as intended.

fix(build): stop next build's workers racing each other's migrations

The release tag failed where three branch builds had passed:

    Collecting page data using 2 workers ...
    SqliteError: database is locked   code: 'SQLITE_BUSY'
      at new <anonymous>              <- the SQLiteAdapter constructor
    Failed to collect page data for /api/ai/chat

`next build` collects page data in several worker processes at once, and each
one imports the route modules — which constructs the db singleton and runs
migrations in its constructor. Pointed at one shared ./data/jade.db they race
to create the same tables. It only bites on a checkout where the file does not
already exist, which is why it was green locally and on earlier CI runs and red
on the first clean release build.

A busy timeout would not have fixed it. Both workers read an empty
__drizzle_migrations BEFORE opening their write transaction, so making them
queue turns "database is locked" into "table users already exists". They must
not share a database at all.

So a production build now gets a private throwaway file per process. The build
has no use for real data — it imports route modules to read their config, not
to query — and an empty database of its own keeps any incidental query working
rather than failing on a missing table. The phase check deliberately precedes
SQLITE_PATH so "a build never opens the real database" holds even for someone
with that variable exported in their shell.

Verified on a clean tree with no data/ present, which is the CI condition:
the build succeeds, 9 workers each get their own jade-build-<pid>.db in
tmpdir, zero SQLITE_BUSY, and ./data is never created at all.

Being straight about the limits of that: reverting the fix and rebuilding under
the same clean conditions did NOT reproduce the failure here — it is a race,
and this machine wins it. The justification is the mechanism, which the CI
stack trace pins precisely, plus the fact that the fix removes the shared
resource by construction rather than making the window smaller.

Related and not addressed: two app instances launched at once (open -n) point
at the same userData database and can race the same migration. That needs
single-instance locking, which is a design decision, not a build fix.

would have missed it on every normal launch and only worked on a slow network.

would otherwise stack ipcRenderer listeners, each firing setState into an
unmounted component.

fix(desktop): allow only one instance to own the data directory

A second launch was not a harmless duplicate window. It started a second Next
server on a different port and opened a second handle on the same SQLite file,
and the two windows stacked on screen — each with its own update panel counting
its own download. That reads as a rendering bug, which is how it was reported,
but nothing was rendering wrong: there were simply two apps.

Two further consequences were already latent and are closed by the same fix.
The port is part of the page origin and Chromium keys localStorage on it, so
whichever instance did not get the stored port silently saw an empty storage
area — the saved API keys look gone in that window. And both instances ran
migrations against one database file, able to race each other exactly as `next
build`'s workers did.

The instance that fails to take the lock quits before initDataPath, before the
settings store, and before any server — it must not open anything the running
instance owns. whenReady still resolves in that process, since quitting is
asynchronous, so the ready handler returns early too. The instance holding the
lock raises and focuses its window on `second-instance`, which is what someone
re-launching an already-running app is asking for.

Verified against the packaged app: three `open -n` launches (which bypass
macOS's own reuse) leave exactly one main process and one Next child, where
before each launch brought up its own server.

The update loop was verified end to end on that same instance while 0.0.3 was
live: 0.0.2 detected it, showed one panel, and downloading produced
261,556,227 bytes in ~/Downloads matching the release exactly, with no .part
left behind. The result mounts, reports version 0.0.3, and its signature
verifies.

feat(db): restore PostgreSQL for the web build, keep the desktop on SQLite

The desktop branch deleted PostgreSQL — adapter, pg-schema, config, four
migrations and their snapshots — because the client never needed it. Merging
that into main would have silently withdrawn a feature the web README
advertises in five places: the feature list, the tech stack table, a documented
Docker recipe, the environment variable table, and the db:generate:pg script.
"Don't wire up PostgreSQL" was about the client, not about dropping it from the
web product.

Two rules now override DB_TYPE instead of trusting it, and both are the caller
refusing an engine rather than choosing a file:

Desktop always uses SQLite. The client's whole promise is that data stays on
the machine, and it inherits whatever environment launched it — a stray
DB_TYPE=postgresql must not send someone's resumes to a server.

A production build always uses SQLite too, into the throwaway per-process file
resolveDatabasePath already returns. `next build` imports every route module to
read its config, which constructs the adapter; against PostgreSQL that means
the build opens a connection to, and runs migrations against, whatever
DATABASE_URL points at — nothing in CI, production in a careless setup. It is
the same reason the build stopped sharing one SQLite file.

That build exemption forced a second one: the "SQLite cannot work on Vercel"
guard is a runtime check, and applying it during a build would fail every
Vercel build of a perfectly correct PostgreSQL app, since the build
deliberately uses SQLite there too.

The restored code keeps this branch's semantics, not main's: a migration
failure still surfaces as a module-load error rather than being swallowed by a
.catch() on dbReady, and a missing DATABASE_URL now says so instead of being
asserted away with a non-null assertion.

Verified against a real PostgreSQL 16 in Docker: migrations applied, all 13
tables created, auto-seed ran, and /api/health, /zh and /api/resume returned
200. Then with JADE_RUNTIME=desktop AND DB_TYPE=postgresql pointed at that same
live server, /api/resume returned userId "local" out of SQLite, and the
PostgreSQL database ended the run with zero tables — never connected. The web
build still produces no ./data directory and no SQLITE_BUSY.

feat(desktop): accept unified v* tags, and only offer installable releases

Groundwork for merging the client into main, where one `v*` tag will drive both
the docker image and the installers instead of a separate `ds-*` line.

parseReleaseTag now accepts `v1.2.3` as well as the legacy `ds-v1.2.3`. Keeping
the old form matters for clients already installed: without it they stop
recognising their own release history the moment the schemes merge.

That change alone would have been actively harmful, and the second half is what
makes it safe. Once `v*` parses, this repo's entire web-only history —
v0.1.0 through v0.4.1, none of which carry installers — outranks a client on
0.0.4 by version number. It would have been told to "update" to a release with
nothing to install. selectAvailableUpdate therefore skips any release without
an installer for this platform AND arch, which reduces the question to the only
one that matters: is there something here I can actually run?

Requiring the asset also makes it impossible for an update to exist that the
user cannot act on, so AvailableUpdate.asset is no longer nullable and the UI's
"no installer, open the release page instead" branch is deleted rather than
left as an unreachable path.

Verified against the live repo: all 30 releases now parse, only the two
carrying installers are eligible, and a client on 0.0.4 is correctly told there
is no update rather than being pushed v0.4.1. Two mutations are caught —
dropping the installer requirement, and dropping ds-v backwards compatibility.

ci: drive both the web image and the desktop installers from one v* tag

Prepares for a single branch and a single release per version. One `v*` tag now
triggers two independent workflow runs — the docker image and the three
installers — so neither can block the other's artifact.

Only desktop-release.yml creates the release. publish.yml's "Create Release"
step is removed: with both triggered by the same tag, they would have raced to
create it, and which one won would decide whether the release carried the
installers at all.

Branch pushes to main no longer package. They still run type-check and tests on
all three platforms, which is the part that has actually caught things — the
Windows run found a test relying on POSIX mode bits, which Windows does not
enforce. Packaging is ~7 minutes per platform on runners billed at 10x Linux,
and the Next build it would exercise is already covered by publish.yml building
the Docker image on the same push, so this buys coverage nothing and costs a
lot.

set-version-from-tag now accepts `v1.2.3` alongside the legacy `ds-v1.2.3`,
using the same shape as parseReleaseTag in the client. The two must agree on

against.

fix(ci): stop pnpm compiling better-sqlite3, which broke the Docker build

Merging the client into main carried its better-sqlite3 12 -> 13 upgrade (done
for Electron's ABI) into the web image, and the Docker build started failing at
`pnpm install` with "Could not find any Python installation to use".

Version 13 has no install script, but it does ship a binding.gyp, and npm/pnpm
default such a package to `node-gyp rebuild` — so listing it in
onlyBuiltDependencies, which was correct for 12 where compiling was the
fallback, now opts it into a compile it never needs. Alpine has no Python, so
only the Docker build noticed; macOS and the GitHub runners have one and
compiled it silently on every install.

It never needed compiling on any of them: 13 ships prebuilt binaries for all
eight triples we target, and there is no build/Release directory even locally —
the prebuild is what has been loading all along.

Verified inside node:22-alpine on both architectures the image is built for,
installing with scripts skipped: zero compiled artifacts, and require +
CREATE TABLE + INSERT + SELECT all work off prebuilds/linuxmusl-*.node.
162 tests still pass locally.

fix(docker): reap Chromium's orphans so PDF export keeps working (#95)

Export works after a restart, stops working some time later, and works again
after another restart. Reproduced against twwch/jadeai:latest.

Every PDF export launches a Chromium. generate-pdf.ts closes it correctly — the
processes really are dead. But as they die, Chromium's helper processes are
re-parented to PID 1, and PID 1 was `node server.js`. Node never calls wait()
on children it did not spawn, so each export left roughly four unreaped zombies
behind.

Zombies hold no memory, which is exactly why the failure is delayed and reads
as random: the container looks healthy, memory sits flat, and nothing is logged
until the PID table fills. From then on Chromium cannot fork and every export
fails — until a restart empties the table and the cycle begins again.

Measured, five exports on the published image:

  4 -> 8 -> 12 -> 16 -> 20 processes, all state Z, all PPID 1
  memory unchanged at 346MB throughout

The same five exports under `docker run --init` left zero, which identified the
missing piece. tini is now baked into the image as PID 1 rather than left to a
flag, because the people hitting this are running the documented command and
have no reason to suspect one they were never told about.

Verified on an image built from this Dockerfile: PID 1 is tini, eight
consecutive exports leave zero zombies and every PDF comes back intact, and
`docker stop` still returns in one second — tini forwards SIGTERM rather than
the daemon timing out and killing the container.
